title: Ladakh's monasteries: etiquette, festivals, routes
meta_description: Visiting Ladakh's gompas: which monasteries to see, morning prayer times, dress and photo rules, and festivals like Hemis Tsechu, Dosmoche and Losar.
summary: Ladakh's gompas are living monasteries, not museums. Visit in the early morning for prayers, dress modestly, walk clockwise, remove shoes and ask before photographs. Thiksey, Hemis, Alchi, Lamayuru and Diskit cover most of the story; time a trip to Hemis Tsechu in summer or Dosmoche and Losar in winter.

sections.heading: A gompa on every ridge
paras: Almost every village in Buddhist Ladakh has a gompa above it, and the reason is practical as much as spiritual. Fields need every flat, irrigated metre of the valley floor, so temples, monks' quarters and chortens go on the rock above. The word gompa itself means a solitary or remote place. Many were built by royal patrons, and their wealth once came from land, grain and the trade caravans passing through Leh.

Most large monasteries belong to one of a few schools of Tibetan Buddhism. Thiksey, Spituk, Likir, Diskit and Karsha are Gelug, the school of the Dalai Lama. Hemis and Stakna follow the Drukpa lineage, and Lamayuru and Phyang belong to the Drikung Kagyu. You do not need to know the differences to enjoy a visit, but your guide will point them out in the paintings and statues.

sections.heading: Which monasteries to see, and when
paras: With a week in Ladakh, five or six gompas are plenty; more and they blur together. We pick them for variety: one for morning prayers, one for art, one for setting, one for a festival or museum. Early morning is the best time almost everywhere: monks gather for prayers, the light is soft and tour groups have not arrived.

sections.heading: How to behave inside
paras: A gompa is a home and a place of worship for the monks who live there. Visitors are welcome, and a few simple habits make you a good guest. Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, and take off hats inside. Remove your shoes where you see others' shoes lined up at the door. Move around chortens, mani walls and prayer wheels clockwise, keeping them on your right.

During prayers, sit at the back or to the side, keep your phone silent and do not walk between monks or in front of the main altar. If a young monk offers butter tea, accept it; you can leave the cup mostly full. A small donation, placed in the box or on the altar, is welcome. Do not touch statues, paintings or ritual objects, and never point your feet at an altar or a seated monk.

sections.heading: What you are looking at inside
paras: Most gompas follow a similar plan, and once you know it, each visit makes more sense. The dukhang is the assembly hall, where monks sit in long rows for prayers facing the main images, with the abbot's raised seat near the front. Pillars are often wrapped in brocade, and long silk banners hang from the ceiling. Smaller temples, called lhakhang, house particular deities, often a large Maitreya, the future Buddha, or Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

The gonkhang is the chapel of the protector deities, usually dark, with masks, weapons and fierce images; some are closed to visitors or to women, and signs will tell you. On the walls, look for the Wheel of Life near the entrance, showing the cycle of rebirth held by a demon, and for mandalas, the circular diagrams used in meditation. Thangkas are painted or embroidered scrolls that can be rolled up and carried; the largest are shown only at festivals.

Outside, chortens hold relics and offerings, and mani walls are built from stones carved with the mantra om mani padme hum. Pass both on your left so they stay on your right. Prayer wheels contain printed mantras; turn them clockwise as you walk past.

sections.heading: Photography rules
paras: Rules vary from room to room and they are enforced. Photography is banned inside Alchi's temples to protect the paintings, and many monasteries forbid it in their main shrines and museums. Flash is never acceptable near old paintings. Where photography is allowed, there may be a small camera fee.

Courtyards, rooftops and exteriors are usually fine. Ask before photographing any monk, nun or villager, and accept a no gracefully. At festivals, do not step into the dance area, block the view of families sitting in front of you or follow masked dancers for a close-up. Drones are restricted in many parts of Ladakh; do not fly one near a monastery without clear permission.

sections.heading: The festival calendar
paras: Monastery festivals follow the Tibetan lunar calendar, so their Gregorian dates move every year. Most include cham, the masked dances performed by monks in the courtyard to drums, cymbals and long horns. They are religious rituals first and spectacles second, and the audience is mostly local families in their best clothes.

Hemis Tsechu, in June or July, is the best known, on the 10th day of the fifth Tibetan month, honouring Padmasambhava. Every twelve years, in the Monkey year, Hemis unrolls its great thangka. In winter, Dosmoche is held below Leh Palace and at Likir and Diskit at the end of the Tibetan year, with a thread-cross offering carried out of town and burnt. Ladakhi Losar, the new year, comes in the eleventh Tibetan month, usually December, two months earlier than in Tibet. Lamayuru, Phyang, Thiksey, Karsha and others have their own festivals through the year. Check current dates with Ladakh tourism before you travel.

sections.heading: Planning a monastery-focused trip
paras: The Indus valley monasteries are at Leh's height, which makes them perfect for your acclimatisation days: Thiksey, Shey and Hemis on day three, then Spituk and Phyang if you want more. A night in the Sham valley at Alchi or Nimmoo adds Likir, Alchi and Basgo at a slightly lower height. Lamayuru deserves a night if you are driving to Kargil; Diskit fits naturally into a Nubra trip.

For festival trips, book Leh rooms and taxis months ahead for Hemis Tsechu. For winter festivals, choose a hotel that stays open with heating, and fly in. Hire a local guide for at least one day: they will read the paintings with you, know when prayers start and help you understand what you are watching. In Leh, guides charge roughly ₹2,000–3,500 a day. Carry a small torch for dark temples, a pair of warm socks for cold floors, and small notes for donations and entry fees. Plan no more than two or three monasteries in a day: the stairs are steep, the halls are dim, and the details are what you came for.

faqs.q: What time are morning prayers at Thiksey?
faqs.a: Morning prayers at Thiksey usually start around 6.30–7 am in summer, with horns sounded from the roof first. Arrive 15 minutes early and sit quietly at the back. Times shift with the season and monastery calendar, so confirm with your hotel or guide the evening before.

faqs.q: What should I wear to visit a monastery in Ladakh?
faqs.a: Cover shoulders and knees, avoid tight or revealing clothes, and remove hats inside temples. Wear shoes that are easy to take off, and warm socks, because floors are cold. A light scarf helps in the sun and for covering up quickly.

faqs.q: Is photography allowed in Ladakh monasteries?
faqs.a: Often not inside shrines and museums, and never at Alchi's temples. Courtyards, rooftops and exteriors are usually fine, sometimes with a small camera fee. Never use flash near paintings, and always ask before photographing monks or local people.

Hemis Tsechu falls on the 10th day of the fifth Tibetan lunar month, usually late June or early July, and lasts two days. Dates move every year. Check current status with Ladakh tourism and book Leh rooms early for festival week.

faqs.q: Which monasteries should I see on a short trip?
faqs.a: With three or four days, see Thiksey for morning prayers, Hemis for its museum, and Alchi for its old paintings. Add Diskit if you go to Nubra, and Lamayuru if you drive towards Kargil. Five well-chosen gompas are better than ten in a rush.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay to enter monasteries?
faqs.a: Most major monasteries charge an entry fee of about ₹25–100 for Indians, sometimes more for foreign nationals and museums. Smaller village gompas may ask only for a donation. Fees change, so carry small notes and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can women visit all parts of a monastery?
faqs.a: Women can visit almost all areas open to tourists. A few protector-deity chapels, called gonkhang, may be closed to women or to all visitors; signs or monks will tell you. Ladakh also has nunneries, and some welcome respectful visitors.

faqs.q: Is it appropriate to give money to monks?
faqs.a: Rather than handing money to individual monks, place a donation in the offering box or on the altar, or buy the entry ticket and a guidebook. If you want to support a monastery's school or nunnery, ask at the office how to give properly.

faqs.q: Are Ladakh's monastery festivals suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes. Children usually enjoy the masks, drums and costumes. Festival days are long and sunny at altitude, so bring hats, water, snacks and cushions, and plan breaks. Keep children seated and out of the dance area at all times.
